title: Line of Sight, Angle of Elevation & Angle of Depression: Physical Optics & Geometric Datum
description: Understand the core optical definitions: Line of Sight, Horizontal Line of Datum, Angle of Elevation (looking upward above horizontal), and Angle of Depression (looking downward below horizontal). Master the Alternate Interior Angles theorem that translates an angle of depression directly into an angle of elevation from the target.
key_concepts: Line of Sight: The straight optical line drawn from the eye of an observer to the target object viewed
Horizontal Datum: The horizontal reference line passing through the observer's eye parallel to the ground
Angle of Elevation: The acute angle formed by the line of sight with the horizontal level when the target is above the horizontal level
Angle of Depression: The acute angle formed by the line of sight with the horizontal level when the target is below the horizontal level
Datum Invariance / Alternate Interior Angles: Since horizontal lines at observer level and ground level are strictly parallel, Angle of Depression = Angle of Elevation to the observer!
subtopics: Optical definitions and eye height considerations
Translating word problems into authentic right-angled triangles
Choosing the right trigonometric ratio: tan θ (Perpendicular/Base) vs sin θ (Perpendicular/Hypotenuse)
Worked Example 1 and Example 2 from NCERT

worked_examples.problem: Example 1 (NCERT): A tower stands vertically on the ground. From a point on the ground, which is 15 m away from the foot of the tower, the angle of elevation of the top of the tower is found to be 60°. Find the height of the tower.
worked_examples.solution:
Let AB be the vertical tower of height 'h' meters, standing on ground.
Let C be the observation point on the ground.
Given: BC = 15 m (Distance from foot of tower).
Angle of elevation ∠ACB = 60°.
Since the tower stands vertically, ∠ABC = 90°.

Step 1: Identify the trigonometric ratio connecting Perpendicular (AB) and Base (BC):
In right-angled triangle ABC:
tan ∠ACB = AB / BC

Step 2: Substitute given values:
tan 60° = h / 15
We know tan 60° = √3:
√3 = h / 15

Step 3: Solve for h:
h = 15√3 m.
[ROUGH_WORK]
If √3 ≈ 1.732, h = 15 × 1.732 = 25.98 m.
In CBSE board exams, keep in exact surd form 15√3 unless √3 is explicitly asked to be approximated.
Boxed Answer: [ Height of tower = 15√3 m ].
concept_questions: Why did we select tan θ instead of sin θ or cos θ in this problem?
What would be the length of the line of sight AC from the observer to the top of the tower?

worked_examples.problem: Example 2 (NCERT): An electrician has to repair an electric fault on a pole of height 5 m. She needs to reach a point 1.3 m below the top of the pole to undertake the repair work. What should be the length of the ladder that she should use which, when inclined at an angle of 60° to the horizontal, would enable her to reach the required position? Also, how far from the foot of the pole should she place the foot of the ladder? (Take √3 = 1.73)
worked_examples.solution:
Let AD be the electric pole of height AD = 5 m.
The repair point B is 1.3 m below the top A:
BD = AD - AB = 5 m - 1.3 m = 3.7 m.
Let BC be the ladder of length 'L' inclined at 60° to horizontal.
In right-angled triangle BDC (right-angled at D):
∠BCD = 60°, BD = 3.7 m.

Step 1: Find ladder length BC (Hypotenuse) using sin 60°:
sin 60° = Opposite / Hypotenuse = BD / BC
√3 / 2 = 3.7 / BC
BC = (3.7 × 2) / √3 = 7.4 / 1.73 ≈ 4.28 m.

Step 2: Find distance of foot of ladder DC (Base) using cot 60° or tan 60°:
cot 60° = Adjacent / Opposite = DC / BD
1 / √3 = DC / 3.7
DC = 3.7 / √3 = 3.7 / 1.73 ≈ 2.14 m.
[ROUGH_WORK]
Check Pythagoras: 2.14² + 3.7² = 4.58 + 13.69 = 18.27 ≈ 4.28² (18.32, verified!).
Boxed Answer: [ Length of ladder = 4.28 m, Distance from foot of pole = 2.14 m ].
concept_questions: Why was the effective height taken as 3.7 m instead of 5 m?
Which ratio connects Perpendicular and Hypotenuse directly?

title: Two-Triangle Systems: Moving Observers, Combined Heights & Shadow Mechanics
description: Master complex scenarios involving two right-angled triangles sharing a common side (either a common height or a common base). Learn how to set up two simultaneous trigonometric equations to eliminate intermediate variables and isolate the unknown tower height or distance.
key_concepts: Common Side Strategy: In two overlapping right triangles, express the common unknown side in terms of the variable from both triangles and equate them
Angular Dynamics: As an observer walks towards a tall object, the angle of elevation monotonically increases (e.g. 30° to 45° to 60°)
Complementary Angles of Elevation: If angles of elevation from distances 'a' and 'b' are complementary (θ and 90° - θ), then height h = √(ab)!
Pedestal & Statue Problems: Height of statue + height of pedestal = Total perpendicular
subtopics: Common height elimination in tandem triangles
Proof of h = √(ab) for complementary elevation angles

worked_examples.problem: Example 6 (NCERT): The angles of depression of the top and the bottom of an 8 m tall building from the top of a multi-storeyed building are 30° and 45°, respectively. Find the height of the multi-storeyed building and the distance between the two buildings.
worked_examples.solution:
Let PC be the multi-storeyed building of height 'H'.
Let AB be the 8 m tall building, so AB = 8 m.
Let distance between buildings BC = d.
Draw horizontal line PD from P parallel to BC, and horizontal line AE from A perpendicular to PC.
Then AE = BC = d, and EC = AB = 8 m.
Therefore, PE = PC - EC = H - 8.

Step 1: In right ΔPAC, ∠PAC = angle of depression of bottom = 45° (by alternate angles):
In right ΔPCB (right-angled at C):
tan 45° = PC / BC = H / d
1 = H / d ⇒ d = H ... (1)
(The distance between the buildings equals the height of the multi-storeyed building!)

Step 2: In right ΔPEA (right-angled at E):
Angle of depression of top of building = 30° ⇒ ∠PAE = 30°.
tan 30° = PE / AE = (H - 8) / d
Substitute d = H from (1):
1 / √3 = (H - 8) / H
H = √3 (H - 8) = H√3 - 8√3
8√3 = H√3 - H = H (√3 - 1)
H = 8√3 / (√3 - 1)

Step 3: Rationalise denominator:
H = [ 8√3 (√3 + 1) ] / [ (√3 - 1)(√3 + 1) ]
= [ 8(3 + √3) ] / [ 3 - 1 ]
= 8(3 + √3) / 2 = 4(3 + √3) = (12 + 4√3) m.
Since d = H, distance between buildings d = 4(3 + √3) m.
[ROUGH_WORK]
If √3 ≈ 1.732: H = 4(4.732) = 18.93 m.
Boxed Answer: [ Height of building = 4(3 + √3) m, Distance between buildings = 4(3 + √3) m ].

worked_examples.problem: Exercise 9.1 Q2: A tree breaks due to storm and the broken part bends so that the top of the tree touches the ground making an angle 30° with it. The distance between the foot of the tree to the point where the top touches the ground is 8 m. Find the height of the tree.
worked_examples.solution:
Let AC be the original unbroken tree.
Suppose the tree broke at point B.
The top part AB bends over to touch the ground at point C'.
Therefore, length of broken part BC' = AB.
Given:
Angle made with ground ∠BC'C = 30°.
Distance from foot of tree C to point of contact C' = CC' = 8 m.
Angle at foot of tree ∠BCC' = 90°.

Total height of the tree = BC + AB = BC + BC'.

Step 1: Find standing part BC in right ΔBCC':
tan 30° = BC / CC'
1 / √3 = BC / 8 ⇒ BC = 8 / √3 m.

Step 2: Find broken part BC' in right ΔBCC':
cos 30° = CC' / BC'
√3 / 2 = 8 / BC' ⇒ BC' = 16 / √3 m.

Step 3: Calculate total tree height:
Total Height = BC + BC' = 8/√3 + 16/√3 = 24 / √3 m.
Rationalise denominator:
= (24 × √3) / (√3 × √3) = 24√3 / 3 = 8√3 m.
[ROUGH_WORK]
If √3 ≈ 1.732: Total height = 8 × 1.732 = 13.856 m.
Boxed Answer: [ Total height of the tree = 8√3 m ].
concept_questions: Why is the height of the tree equal to Perpendicular + Hypotenuse?
Could we have used Pythagoras theorem to find BC' after finding BC?

worked_examples.problem: Exercise 9.1 Q6: A 1.5 m tall boy is standing at some distance from a 30 m tall building. The angle of elevation from his eyes to the top of the building increases from 30° to 60° as he walks towards the building. Find the distance he walked towards the building.
worked_examples.solution:
Let AB be the tall building of height AB = 30 m.
Let CD be the boy of height CD = 1.5 m at initial position, and C'D' be his position after walking.
Draw horizontal line through his eyes D-D'-E meeting the building at E.
Then BE = 1.5 m.
Effective height AE = AB - BE = 30 - 1.5 = 28.5 m = 57 / 2 m.

Let the initial angle of elevation be ∠ADE = 30°.
Let the final angle of elevation be ∠AD'E = 60°.
Distance walked = DD' = DE - D'E.

Step 1: In right ΔAD'E (right-angled at E):
tan 60° = AE / D'E
√3 = 28.5 / D'E ⇒ D'E = 28.5 / √3 m.

Step 2: In right ΔADE (right-angled at E):
tan 30° = AE / DE
1 / √3 = 28.5 / DE ⇒ DE = 28.5√3 m.

Step 3: Distance walked by the boy:
DD' = DE - D'E = 28.5√3 - 28.5 / √3
= 28.5 [ √3 - 1/√3 ] = 28.5 [ (3 - 1) / √3 ] = 28.5 × (2 / √3) = 57 / √3 m.
Rationalise denominator:
DD' = 57√3 / 3 = 19√3 m.
[ROUGH_WORK]
57 / 3 = 19.
19 × √3 ≈ 19 × 1.732 = 32.91 m.
Boxed Answer: [ Distance walked towards building = 19√3 m ].
concept_questions: Why did we subtract 1.5 m from 30 m at the beginning?
What happens to the angle of elevation as the observer gets infinitely close to the building?

worked_examples.problem: Exercise 9.1 Q10: Two poles of equal heights are standing opposite each other on either side of the road, which is 80 m wide. From a point between them on the road, the angles of elevation of the top of the poles are 60° and 30°, respectively. Find the height of the poles and the distances of the point from the poles.
worked_examples.solution:
Let AB and CD be the two poles of equal height 'h', so AB = CD = h.
Let BD be the 80 m wide road, BD = 80 m.
Let P be the observation point on the road between B and D.
Let BP = x meters, then PD = 80 - x meters.
Given angles of elevation:
∠APB = 60° and ∠CPD = 30°.
Both poles stand vertically: ∠ABP = ∠CDP = 90°.

Step 1: In right ΔABP (right-angled at B):
tan 60° = AB / BP
√3 = h / x ⇒ h = x√3 ... (1)

Step 2: In right ΔCDP (right-angled at D):
tan 30° = CD / PD
1 / √3 = h / (80 - x)
80 - x = h√3 ... (2)

Step 3: Substitute h = x√3 into equation (2):
80 - x = (x√3) × √3
80 - x = 3x
80 = 4x ⇒ x = 20 m.

Step 4: Compute distances and pole height:
Distance from Pole AB: BP = x = 20 m.
Distance from Pole CD: PD = 80 - x = 80 - 20 = 60 m.
Height of the poles: h = x√3 = 20√3 m.
[ROUGH_WORK]
Check in ΔCDP: tan 30° = 20√3 / 60 = √3 / 3 = 1/√3 (Verified!).
If √3 ≈ 1.732: h = 20 × 1.732 = 34.64 m.
Boxed Answer: [ Height of poles = 20√3 m, Distances of point = 20 m and 60 m ].
concept_questions: Why is the closer pole (20 m away) associated with the steeper angle 60°?
What would be the height if the point was exactly at the midpoint of the road?

title: Exercise 9.1 Part 3 Solver: Cable Towers, Ships, Aeroplanes & Complementary Heights (Q12 to Q16)
description: Exhaustive resolution of NCERT Exercise 9.1 Questions 12 through 16. Covers cable tower from 7 m building (Q12), two ships observed from 75 m lighthouse with angles of depression 30° and 45° (Q13), 1.2 m girl spotting 88.2 m balloon moving horizontally (Q14), highway tower and car accelerating towards tower foot taking 6 seconds (Q15), and the landmark proof for complementary angles of elevation h = √(ab) (Q16).
key_concepts: Ex 9.1 Q12: 7 m building to cable tower (elevation 60°, depression 45°) ⇒ Tower height = 7(√3 + 1) m
Ex 9.1 Q13: 75 m lighthouse, depression of two ships 30° and 45° ⇒ Distance between ships = 75(√3 - 1) m
Ex 9.1 Q14: 1.2 m girl and 88.2 m balloon: Effective height = 87 m; angle changes 60° to 30° ⇒ Distance traveled = 58√3 m
Ex 9.1 Q15: Car moving towards tower with uniform speed: Depression changes from 30° to 60° in 6 seconds ⇒ Time to reach foot = 3 seconds!
Ex 9.1 Q16: Complementary angles of elevation from distances a and b: tan θ = h/a and tan(90° - θ) = cot θ = h/b ⇒ h² = ab ⇒ h = √(ab) = √(4 × 9) = 6 m
subtopics: Complete resolution of Q12 to Q16 with rigorous algebraic proofs
Uniform speed kinematics coupled with trigonometry (Q15)
Full algebraic proof of complementary heights formula h = √(ab)

worked_examples.problem: Exercise 9.1 Q15: A straight highway leads to the foot of a tower. A man standing at the top of the tower observes a car at an angle of depression of 30°, which is approaching the foot of the tower with a uniform speed. Six seconds later, the angle of depression of the car is found to be 60°. Find the time taken by the car to reach the foot of the tower from this point.
worked_examples.solution:
Let AB be the tower of height 'h'.
Let the car be initially at point C with angle of depression 30°.
By alternate interior angles, ∠ACB = 30°.
Six seconds later, the car reaches point D with angle of depression 60°.
By alternate interior angles, ∠ADB = 60°.
Let 'v' be the uniform speed of the car in m/s.
Distance CD covered in 6 seconds = Speed × Time = 6v meters.
Let 't' be the time taken by the car to travel from D to B.
Then distance DB = v × t meters.

Step 1: In right ΔABD (right-angled at B):
tan 60° = AB / DB = h / (vt)
√3 = h / (vt) ⇒ h = vt√3 ... (1)

Step 2: In right ΔABC (right-angled at B):
tan 30° = AB / BC = h / (CD + DB) = h / (6v + vt)
1 / √3 = h / [ v(6 + t) ]
h√3 = v(6 + t) ... (2)

Step 3: Substitute h = vt√3 from (1) into (2):
(vt√3) × √3 = v(6 + t)
3vt = 6v + vt
Divide both sides by v (since speed v > 0):
3t = 6 + t
2t = 6 ⇒ t = 3 seconds!
[ROUGH_WORK]
Notice speed 'v' cancels out completely! The geometry forces the remaining distance DB to be exactly half of distance CD (since cot 30° - cot 60° = √3 - 1/√3 = 2/√3, while cot 60° = 1/√3).
Boxed Answer: [ Time taken to reach the foot of the tower = 3 seconds ].

worked_examples.problem: Exercise 9.1 Q16: The angles of elevation of the top of a tower from two points at a distance of 4 m and 9 m from the base of the tower and in the same straight line with it are complementary. Prove that the height of the tower is 6 m.
worked_examples.solution:
Let AB be the tower of height 'h'.
Let C and D be two points on the ground in the same straight line as base B.
Given:
BC = 4 m, BD = 9 m.
Angles of elevation are complementary:
Let ∠ACB = θ, then ∠ADB = 90° - θ.

Step 1: In right ΔABC (right-angled at B):
tan θ = AB / BC = h / 4 ... (1)

Step 2: In right ΔABD (right-angled at B):
tan(90° - θ) = AB / BD = h / 9
Recall the complementary angle identity: tan(90° - θ) = cot θ:
cot θ = h / 9 ... (2)

Step 3: Multiply equation (1) and equation (2):
tan θ × cot θ = (h / 4) × (h / 9)
We know tan θ × cot θ = tan θ × (1 / tan θ) = 1:
1 = h² / 36
h² = 36
h = √36 = 6 m (taking positive root since height cannot be negative).

Hence Proved that the height of the tower is 6 m!
[ROUGH_WORK]
General theorem: For complementary angles from distances a and b, h = √(ab).
Here a = 4, b = 9 ⇒ h = √(4 × 9) = √36 = 6 m.
Boxed Answer: [ Height of tower = 6 m (Proved) ].

Would this formula hold if the distances were 3 m and 12 m? What would the height be?
